summary: This applicability statement covers when IPv6 UDP datagrams may use a zero checksum. It gives recommendations and requirements, describes the issues and design principles for UDP tunnels over IPv6, and examines the role of the IPv6 UDP checksum. It also notes constraints on network paths that include middleboxes.

eli5.summary: Skipping a safety check is only okay in some cases. This lays out when it is fine and what can go wrong, especially with in-between network gear.

questions: when is zero udp checksum allowed in ipv6
when is a zero udp checksum allowed in ipv6
why does ipv6 need a udp checksum
can middleboxes drop zero checksum udp
subtitle: When an IPv6 tunnel may skip the UDP checksum, and the rules that make it safe enough.

tldr.problem: IPv6 has no header checksum, so the UDP checksum is the only thing catching misdelivered or corrupted datagrams. Some tunnel protocols, already running over IPv4 with no UDP checksum, want to skip it for IPv6 too.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC says when a zero UDP checksum may be used and sets rules for end hosts, for the protocols that use it and for middleboxes: enable it only per port, keep integrity checks above UDP, probe the path, and fall back to a real checksum.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard that works alongside RFC 6935. The RFC's own advice is to try a normal checksum or UDP-Lite first and use a zero checksum only when the constraints allow.

facts.label: Fast-path bytes seen by some routers

today: RFC 6936 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It accompanies RFC 6935, which changes the IPv6 rule, and it cites RFC 2460 as the specification it relates to.

sections.title: Why a Zero Checksum Is a Question
sections.content:
RFC 2460 requires IPv6 senders to compute a non-zero UDP checksum. IPv6 has no header checksum of its own, so the checksum, which covers a pseudo-header with the addresses, also gives a statistical check that a datagram reached the intended destination. IPv4 does not have this problem because its header checksum already protects the addresses.

Certain tunnel applications already run over IPv4 with a zero UDP checksum and want the same for IPv6. RFC 6936 is an applicability statement: it does not itself change IPv6 (that is RFC 6935), it says when and how the zero checksum method may be used. Its conclusion is that a zero checksum is the best of the proposed alternatives for the goals of certain tunnel applications, but only under constraints.
sections.eli5: On IPv6 the UDP checksum is the main way to notice a letter went to the wrong house. Some tunnels want to skip it, so the rulebook says when that is allowed.

sections.title: Why Tunnels Want to Skip It
sections.content:
A tunnel wraps another protocol's packets inside UDP datagrams. Several motivations are listed for a simpler checksum rule:

  • Lower forwarding cost, because the inner packet is often already protected by its own checksum.
  • No need to read the whole packet. Many router forwarding engines see only the first n bytes of a packet, typically n <= 128, so checksumming a large packet is poorly suited to them.
  • Better behavior through middleboxes, since many handle UDP but not UDP-Lite.
  • A wish to keep UDP port numbers for load sharing.

Automatic Multicast Tunneling (AMT) is an example. It must replicate a multicast packet to each gateway tunnel, and each tunnel has different outer addresses, so a different pseudo-header would have to be built for each copy.

The RFC also discusses using the IPv6 flow label for load balancing instead of ports, but notes that many endpoints set it to zero and that a tunnel ingress would need extra state to fill it in well.
sections.eli5: Checking every box in a huge truck takes time. Tunnels that already have a label inside each box would like to skip checking the outer wrapping too.

sections.title: The Standards-Track Alternatives
sections.content:
Before using a zero checksum, designers should look at what already exists. UDP with a checksum has close to universal support and verifies the address and port, but some devices cannot checksum a full datagram efficiently. UDP-Lite (RFC 3828) can limit checksum coverage to the headers, but it uses a different Next Header value, so few middleboxes understand it. General tunnels such as IP-in-IP and GRE have no or optional checksums and use their own Next Header value, which makes it less likely that a corrupted packet is delivered to an application.

The RFC warns that IPv6 with a zero UDP checksum is not the same as IPv4 with a zero UDP checksum, and that designers should not be fooled into thinking so. For some sets of constraints no solution exists, and the recommendation is then to use or fall back to UDP with full checksum coverage.
sections.eli5: There are other ways to send a package, like a simpler envelope or a plain box. Pick the zero checksum only if none of those fit.

sections.title: What Can Go Wrong Without a Checksum
sections.content:
Without a checksum, corruption that IPv4's header checksum would catch goes unnoticed in IPv6. The RFC walks through the cases:

  • Destination address corrupted: the datagram may reach a different host, and without a checksum it is passed on to any application bound to the port.
  • Source address corrupted: the datagram is usually processed in the right context with wrong origin information, which can create needless state (RTP is the example) or misdirect ICMP messages.
  • Ports corrupted: data or errors may reach the wrong application process.
  • Fragmentation fields corrupted: a fragment can join the wrong packet, giving erroneous reassembly. This risk grows with recursive tunneling.

UDP is more exposed than connection-oriented transports because it has no handshake or sequence numbers, and applications often bind to wildcard values. A protocol using a zero checksum cannot assume it is the only one doing so, so it must handle misdelivered or malformed packets gracefully.

Middleboxes are a second problem. RFC 2460 disallows a zero checksum, so a firewall or NAT that validates or rewrites the checksum may drop such datagrams. A sender therefore needs to probe the path, and a zero checksum arriving from the remote end does not prove that it can also receive one.
sections.eli5: Without the check, a letter with a smudged address might be opened by the wrong person, and the wrong person might act on it. Routes can also change, so you keep testing that your skipped-check mail still gets through.

sections.title: Requirements for IPv6 Nodes
sections.content:
Section 4 lists ten requirements for nodes that support the method. The main ones:

  • Nodes SHOULD, by default, NOT allow zero checksums for transmission.
  • Nodes MUST let an application choose the set of ports enabled to send, and the set enabled to receive, zero-checksum datagrams.
  • Nodes MUST let an application require a calculated checksum on a particular datagram at any time, for example for keepalives.
  • The default receiver behavior MUST be to discard datagrams with a zero UDP checksum.
  • Ports with the method enabled MUST also accept datagrams with a calculated checksum, using the RFC 2460 method when the field is not zero.
  • Ports with the method enabled MUST NOT log a datagram just because its checksum is zero.
  • ICMPv6 messages that refer to zero-checksum packets MUST be checked for consistency before the node acts on them.

Enabling per port rather than per interface matters: otherwise every UDP application on the node would start receiving unverified datagrams.
sections.eli5: The rule is that the skip-the-check mode starts switched off, and an app has to ask for it for one specific mailbox. Everyone else keeps getting the normal safe treatment.

sections.title: Rules for Protocols and Middleboxes
sections.content:
Section 5 begins by telling protocol developers to seriously consider checksummed UDP or UDP-Lite first. If a protocol does use the zero checksum, it:

  • MUST enable it only for a specific port or port range, at both ends.
  • Is RECOMMENDED to keep an integrity mechanism at the transported layer. A tunnel carrying IP packets MAY rely on inner checks if it does not significantly increase corruption; otherwise it MUST add its own.
  • MUST be designed so corrupted headers do not cause incorrect state to accumulate.
  • MUST have a CRC or similar check if it carries non-IP payloads, unless the payload suits a lower layer without integrity guarantees.
  • SHOULD send keepalives with a zero checksum, and SHOULD include both checksummed and zero-checksum keepalives so the peer can tell path failure from dropping of zero-checksum datagrams.

A middlebox MUST forward IPv6 UDP datagrams with either a zero or a standard checksum on the same port, and MUST NOT keep separate flow state depending on the checksum value. It MAY restrict zero-checksum forwarding to configured port ranges.

For tunnel routers that cannot reach the payload, both ends must be configured for a zero checksum (including turning off hardware checksum offload), middleboxes on the path must be updated, and the egress should use source address filtering and rate-limiting.
sections.eli5: An app using the skip mode has to keep its own lock on what it sends, keep testing that the road still allows it, and have a fallback plan. Gatekeepers on the road must not treat the two kinds of mail as different conversations.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Transport checksums are the first stage of protection for the stack, though they are not authentication. They also keep packet counters honest and help detect unusual behavior.

If a tunnel egress handles zero-checksum packets much faster than checksummed ones, an attacker could inject non-zero checksummed packets to overload the slow path. The RFC suggests source-address filtering and throttling, though throttling may affect the tunnel protocol. Probing the path, and sending zero-checksum packets at all, could also reveal information that helps an on-path attacker identify the operating system or tunnel type.

Because general tunnels such as IP-in-IP or GRE present a large attack surface, firewalls may be configured to block them. For that reason this statement allows the method only for specific port ranges.
sections.eli5: A fast lane with no inspection can be flooded by someone sending slow-to-check packages. Guards at the door and a limit on how many can come in help.
